t.6.97.1: Then, at that moment, Mātali reminded Rāghava: "Why, O hero, do you merely follow his lead, as though you did not know?"
t.6.97.2: Release the weapon of the Grandsire, O lord, for his slaying; the time of his destruction, which was foretold by the gods, has arrived today.
t.6.97.3: Then Rāma, reminded by those words of Mātali, took up a blazing arrow that was like a hissing serpent.
t.6.97.4: The great arrow fashioned by Brahmā, unfailing in battle, which the mighty and venerable sage Agastya had first bestowed upon him.
t.6.97.6: In its feathers was the Wind, in its head were Fire and the Sun, its body was made of the sky, and in its weight were Meru and Mandara.
t.6.97.5: It had been fashioned long ago by Brahmā of boundless might for the sake of Indra, and was formerly given to the lord of the gods when he longed for victory over the three worlds.
t.6.97.7: Blazing in its very form, finely feathered and adorned with gold, it had been fashioned from the splendor of all beings and shone with the brilliance of the sun.
t.6.97.8: It was like the smoking fire of Time at the world's end, like a blazing venomous serpent, swift in action, a shatterer of hosts of chariots, elephants and horses.
t.6.97.9: That arrow could shatter gates, iron bars, and even mountains; its shaft was drenched with the blood of many creatures, smeared with fat, and exceedingly dreadful.
t.6.97.10: Hard as the thunderbolt and loudly roaring, terrible in many a battle, terrifying to all and dreadful, it was like a hissing serpent.
t.6.97.11: Yama-like in form and bringing terror, it was the one that ever provided food in battle to the flocks of herons and vultures and to the packs of jackals and rākṣasas.
t.6.97.12: It was the gladdener of the monkey-chiefs and the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, feathered with the many lovely and variegated feathers of Garutmant.
t.6.97.13: That supreme arrow, destroyer of the fear of the worlds and of the Ikṣvākus, robber of the glory of his foes, and bringer of joy to himself.
t.6.97.14: Then the mighty Rāma, of great strength, having consecrated that great arrow with mantras according to the rite declared in the Veda, fitted it to his bow.
t.6.97.15: Greatly enraged, drawing his bow with all his might and summoning his utmost effort, he loosed that supreme arrow, which strikes the vital parts, at Rāvaṇa.
t.6.97.17: That arrow, once released, of great velocity and bringing an end to the body, pierced the heart of that evil-souled Rāvaṇa.
t.6.97.16: Released by the one whose arms were like thunderbolts, that arrow, as unassailable as the thunderbolt and as irresistible as Death itself, fell upon Rāvaṇa's chest.
t.6.97.18: That arrow, smeared with blood and bringing an end to life, carried away the life-breaths of Rāvaṇa and with great force entered the surface of the earth.
t.6.97.19: That arrow, having slain Rāvaṇa, its surface made wet with blood, its task accomplished, entered its own quiver again as if humbly.
t.6.97.20: From the hand of him who had been struck down, as he was falling away from life, that bow together with its arrows swiftly fell, along with his life-breaths.
t.6.97.21: And the lord of the Nairṛtas, of terrible speed and great splendour, now lifeless, fell from his chariot to the ground, like Vṛtra struck down by the thunderbolt.
t.6.97.22: Seeing him fallen upon the ground, the night-wanderers who remained of the slain, their lord killed and themselves stricken with fear, fled in all directions.
t.6.97.23: Having seen the slaying of Daśagrīva and the victory of Rāghava, the vānaras, who fight with trees, roared and fell upon them.
t.6.97.24: Harried by the exultant monkeys, they fled in fear toward Laṅkā, their protector slain, their faces piteous and streaming with tears.
t.6.97.25: Then the monkeys, overjoyed and flushed with victory, roared aloud, proclaiming the triumph of Rāghava and that slaying of Rāvaṇa.
t.6.97.26: Then in the sky the gentle kettledrum of the gods resounded, and there blew a most pleasant breeze bearing heavenly fragrance.
t.6.97.28: And in the sky was heard the excellent voice of the great-souled deities, joined with praise of Rāghava, crying, "Well done, well done!"
t.6.97.27: Then from the sky a shower of flowers fell upon the earth, strewing Rāghava's chariot with blossoms rare and lovely.
t.6.97.29: When the fierce Rāvaṇa, who struck terror into all the worlds, was slain, a great joy entered the gods together with the Cāraṇas.
t.6.97.30: Then Rāghava, delighted, having slain that bull among rākṣasas, made Sugrīva and the mighty Aṅgada fulfilled in their desire.
t.6.97.32: Then Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa and the other foremost friends, together with Lakṣmaṇa, rejoicing at the victory, gathered round Rāghava, delightful in battle, and honored him with due rites.
t.6.97.31: Then the hosts of Maruts became calm, the quarters grew clear, and the sky became spotless. The earth no longer trembled, nor did the winds blow, and the sun, too, shone with a steady radiance.
t.6.97.33: Then that mighty son of the kings of Raghu's line, firm in his vow, his enemy slain, shone on the battlefield surrounded by the forces of his own people, like Indra encircled by the hosts of the gods.
